facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Some says Raja Bhoj of Malwa, who ruled between 1076 to 1099 AD, built the temple while another theory is that the temple was built in the eight century by Adi Shankracharya.
facts.source_name: Down To Earth / Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: Historical opinions diverge on the construction of the masonry shrine, with some traditions attributing it to the 8th-century revivalist Adi Shankara while others credit King Bhoja of Malwa in the 11th century or regional Katyuri kings.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Kedarnath Temple is dated to around 1050 AD by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) though it is generally believed to be more ancient.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India dates the standing stone edifice of the Kedarnath temple to approximately 1050 CE based on its structural and stylistic attributes.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The domes of the temple are interlocked with each other using iron clamps; that is why they are intact. Only loose and cracked stones of the temple have come out.
facts.text: Structural investigations by the Archaeological Survey of India found that the temple survived the flood forces because its dry ashlar granite blocks were joined with iron clamps and interlocking ball-and-socket joints without mortar.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Striations on the wall of the temple, which could have formed when the glacier moved around the structure, further supports the finding.
facts.text: A geological examination by researchers at the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology identified yellowish glacial striations and polished facets across the masonry blocks of the temple.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Ravinder identified four well-defined moraine loops present at altitudes of 3,160 m, 3,320 m, 3,440 m, and 3,640 m.
facts.text: Lichenometric measuring of Rhizocarpon geographicum by the Wadia Institute identified four well-defined Chorabari moraine loops at elevations ranging from 3160 to 3640 metres.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It is evident that the huge boulder, which is 10 feet high and little over 30 feet in length prevented the flow of moraine and floods into the temple premises.
facts.text: Field documentation by the Archaeological Survey of India confirmed that a giant boulder measuring over 30 feet long and 10 feet high came to rest directly behind the temple during the June 2013 flood.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: TV footage shows that a huge boulder, among the largest in the debris, had landed a few metres from the rear of the temple, splitting the flow of water and protecting the rear of the shrine from much of its fury.
facts.text: Post-disaster geological site inspections reported that the massive boulder acted as a natural breakwater, splitting the descending torrent of mud and rocks into two flows that bypassed the temple on either flank.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Mani said it has been corroborated that the Ishaan temple was washed away in the floods... Minor damage to outer wall of Kedarnath sanctum
facts.text: A detailed conservation survey by the Archaeological Survey of India established that although surrounding residential structures and the nearby Ishaan temple were obliterated, the core sanctum of Kedarnath remained structurally undamaged.
